One of the most expensive habits in trading is answering “Why am I still holding this?” with a description of what the company does.

Great business. Huge growth potential. The leader in its industry. You might be right about all of it. But that still doesn’t explain whether your entry made sense, whether your position is too large, or whether the setup you bought is still there.

A good company can still be a bad trade.

I think a lot of traders get into trouble because they mix together three separate decisions: finding a business worth following, finding a setup worth buying, and deciding how much money to put behind it. Being right about the first one doesn’t automatically make the other two good decisions.

For me, a strong company earns a place on the watchlist. Then I look for relative strength, both in the stock itself and in its group. Is the stock outperforming the market? Is it holding up well during pullbacks? Are other names in the same theme or industry showing strength too?

A strong stock within a strong group gives me more confidence that I’m seeing broader demand. That matters when choosing where to put my capital. Plenty of companies are interesting, but I want to focus on the leaders.

Then I still need the price structure, entry, and risk to make sense. Relative strength helps me decide what to focus on; it doesn’t make every price a good entry. I can love a name and still have nothing to do with it for weeks because the opportunity doesn’t fit my process.

The harder part comes after you’re in.

Say I buy a pullback into a rising 21 EMA, with strong stock and group RS, expecting the stock to hold its structure and resume higher. Before entering, I should know what would invalidate that setup and how I’ll handle it. If that happens, “but earnings are growing 80%” doesn’t resolve the problem. Those earnings were already part of the story when I planned the trade.

This is where a swing trade can quietly become a long-term investment. The stock moves against you, and suddenly you’re talking about where the business will be in five years. The timeframe changes, the stop disappears, and the position stays the same size.

You’re allowed to have a long-term thesis. But that thesis deserves its own plan and sizing. It shouldn’t appear for the first time when you don’t want to take a loss.

I also think a lot of disagreement about a stock comes down to people talking about different timeframes without realizing it. Someone sees me exit and responds, "Why will the company be much bigger in five years?" That may be true. I’m a swing trader. My position was built around an opportunity over the coming days or weeks, and that opportunity may have changed.

We can agree on the quality of the business and still make completely different decisions with the stock. A long-term investor and a swing trader don’t need the same entry, the same pullback tolerance, or the same reason to exit.

Selling doesn’t mean I suddenly think the company is bad. It means I no longer want that exposure within the timeframe and setup I’m trading. I can keep following it, let the structure rebuild, watch for renewed relative strength, and buy it again.

And yes, sometimes you exit, and the stock turns right back up. That’s frustrating. But holding every failed setup to avoid that frustration comes with its own cost.

The question I want to answer is: “Does this position still deserve this much of my capital, based on the plan I’m trading?”

That’s a much more useful question than “Do I still like the company?”

You don’t need to stop believing in a company to stop holding its stock.

When a stock catches your attention, how often do you look at what the rest of its group is doing?

That’s a big part of my process. I want to know whether I’ve found an isolated move or a stock participating in something broader. Are its peers also showing relative strength? Are several names building constructive bases, holding their pullbacks, and starting to move higher?

One stock moving on company-specific news can absolutely produce a good trade. But when several names within a theme start acting well together, that gives me another reason to investigate. A broader shift in where money is going may be underway.

This is how I use ThemesLab inside TradersLab. I start with the groups to see where strength is developing, then work down to the individual stocks. It helps me put a name in context before getting attached to its chart or its story.

I care about two layers of relative strength: how the group is behaving relative to the market, and how the stock is behaving relative to the market and its peers. If the market pulls back, which groups hold up? Within those groups, which stocks give up the least ground? When conditions improve, which ones respond first?

Those observations help me narrow my watchlist. Then I need an entry.

A leading stock in a leading group can still be extended, difficult to size, or too far from a logical stop. For my style, I’m usually looking for a controlled pullback into rising structure where I can define the risk. Group strength and stock strength help me choose where to look; the setup determines whether there’s a trade to take.

And if several names from the same theme make the list, I have to remember that they may all move together. Five attractive charts can still leave me heavily exposed to the same underlying move.

That’s the workflow behind how I use TradersLab: assess the market, explore the groups, narrow down the stocks, then decide whether the entry and risk make sense.

Debt trap and inflation end-game.

The biggest medium- to long-term problem I see is that the system increasingly depends on the same things that are making the underlying problem worse: lower rates, more liquidity and more fiscal support.

The fiscal starting point is already uncomfortable. CBO projects roughly $7.4T of federal spending against $5.6T of revenue in 2026, leaving a ~$1.9T deficit. 

In other words, roughly 26 cents of every dollar Washington spends is borrowed. Debt held by the public is already around 101% of GDP. 

The latest numbers are even more striking. Through August, the government spent $6.81T, collected $4.85T, and ran a $1.97T deficit. 

Net interest alone reached $1.05T, up 12% YoY, equivalent to roughly 22% of all federal revenue collected. 

That creates a huge growth hurdle. With roughly $32T of public debt and a ~$1.9T annual deficit, the economy needs approximately 6% nominal GDP growth per year simply to keep debt-to-GDP from deteriorating further, assuming the deficit stays constant.

Actually growing out of the deficit is much harder. Federal revenue is about 17.5% of GDP. At that same tax take, generating another $1.9T of annual revenue would require roughly $10.9T of additional GDP, about 34% cumulative nominal growth from today’s economy, and that assumes federal spending somehow stops growing while the economy catches up. 

Now imagine the next recession requires another $4T fiscal response.

At 4% financing, that creates $160B of additional interest every year. At 5%, it is $200B every year. And that is before refinancing the existing debt.

This is where the feedback loop becomes dangerous.

A recession requires stimulus. Stimulus requires borrowing. Borrowing increases debt and Treasury supply. More debt increases interest expense. Higher interest expense increases the deficit. Larger deficits require still more borrowing.

But there is another problem: the borrowing itself can make the recovery harder.

Normally, recessions bring falling long-term yields, making mortgages, corporate debt, refinancing and investment cheaper. But if enormous deficits and Treasury issuance keep long-term yields elevated, the private economy may not receive as much of that traditional relief. CBO explicitly notes that greater federal borrowing can push up economy-wide interest rates, crowd out private investment and slow economic growth. 

So you can end up with an uncomfortable cycle:

Weak economy → fiscal stimulus → more debt → higher long-term yields → expensive mortgages and corporate credit → less investment and demand → harder recovery.

The Fed can cut short-term rates, but that does not guarantee that 10-, 20- or 30-year borrowing costs fall with them. We are seeing this fight currently being fought with the market front running the rate hikes and the FED following.

That is what makes the next recession potentially different. The government may need to spend trillions to pull the economy out of a downturn while the financing required to do so simultaneously keeps the cost of capital elevated.

CBO already projects net interest rising from roughly $1T today to $2.1T by 2036, while public debt rises from 101% to 120% of GDP, without assuming any emergency. 

At some point, part of the medicine can begin working against the cure.

This is a global issue with yields spiking across all major economies. We are facing a global debt crisis, out of which the only logical way out will be inflation, probably running at 3-4% rather than the widely accepted and believed 2% target.

The biggest context is that this is an AI bull market, the 4th industrial revolution of humankind. I believe we are still very early in this generational bull market.

I can't be you, and you wouldn't want to be me.
